edges.note: An aggregate is a cluster of entities plus value objects; value objects are the immutable building blocks held inside it.
Repositories provide access to aggregate roots; conventionally one repository per aggregate type.

edges.cite: Vernon, Implementing DDD (2013), Event Sourcing; Fowler event sourcing
edges.note: Event-sourced systems persist an aggregate's state as its stream of domain events and rebuild it by replay.
Aggregates raise domain events on state changes as the mechanism for propagating consistency across boundaries.
A diagnostic/mapped context (MDC) is a context object specialized to carry per-request diagnostic key-values along the call path.
Both supply ambient execution-scoped state: pass it explicitly in a context object vs stash it in thread-local storage.
Interceptors/filters in a processing chain receive and enrich a shared context object carrying request state.
Client hydration re-runs components to build a virtual DOM and reconciles it against the existing server-rendered DOM.
Hydration re-establishes event listeners and data bindings over static server markup so the UI becomes interactive.
Fine-grained frameworks (e.g. Solid) hydrate by attaching signal-driven effects to existing server DOM nodes.
Making a value immutable removes the need for defensive copying to guard against alias mutation.
Immutable values can be freely shared; copy-on-write gives cheap logical mutation by copying only on change.
Persistent structures are built from immutable nodes shared unchanged across successive versions.
Signals typically hold immutable values swapped wholesale on update, so equality checks detect real changes.
Given a shared reference, keep the value truly immutable or allow controlled runtime-checked mutation via interior mutability.
Rc<RefCell<T>> combines shared ownership (refcount) with interior mutation behind an immutable shared reference.
Signal implementations use interior mutability to store state behind shared immutable handles.

edges.cite: Bernier, Latency Compensating Methods in Client/Server In-game Protocol Design (Valve, 2001)
edges.note: Valve netcode combines client-side input prediction with server-side lag compensation (rewind) as complementary parts.
The server uses recorded entity-history snapshots to rewind to where the client (which interpolates) saw targets.
Two latency strategies: authoritative server-side rewind of history vs peer deterministic predict-and-rollback.
On server rejection the optimistically-applied local state is rolled back to the last confirmed value.
Client-side optimism pairs with server-side OCC version checks that adjudicate whether the write actually succeeds.
The optimistic change mutates local bound state so the UI re-renders immediately before confirmation.
Encode reactive behavior as forward-chained condition-action rules vs as explicit states and transitions.
Competing structures for AI/decision logic: engine-driven production rules vs a ticked tree of composable nodes.
Individual rule conditions are naturally expressed as composable specification predicates over working state.

edges.cite: Samek, Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++ (PSiCC2), ch.2
edges.note: A state machine processes each event fully (run-to-completion) before dequeuing the next, never observed mid-transition.
Events are buffered in a queue and dispatched one at a time to preserve run-to-completion semantics.
Events that cannot be handled in the current state are deferred and re-dispatched in a later RTC step.
A reminder posts an event to the machine itself, handled in the next run-to-completion step to continue processing.
Executed operations are recorded as Command objects supporting unexecute, pushed onto a history stack.
Commands store pre-operation state as mementos so the stack can revert without knowing internal structure.
The Command Processor component manages the command history and provides the undo/redo mechanism.
Revert/reconstruct state via inverse-command replay off a local stack vs replaying a durable event log.
Lockstep stalls until all inputs arrive (no misprediction); prediction advances immediately and reconciles later.
Rollback saves periodic simulation-state snapshots (mementos) to restore when a predicted remote input proves wrong.
Two ways to render remote entities between updates: extrapolate from last kinematics vs interpolate between snapshots.
Two implementations of statechart concurrent (AND) regions: decomposed coordinated machines vs contained orthogonal components.

edges.cite: Douglass, Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C (2010), state machine patterns
edges.note: Two FSM implementation choices: one parameterized event-receptor function vs one function per event type.
Two FSM realizations: encode state by which per-state collection holds the object vs by swapping method/delegate references.
Change detection strategies: fine-grained dependency tracking that re-runs exactly affected computations vs a compare-until-stable check loop.
UI update strategies: fine-grained signal propagation to exact DOM nodes vs diffing a re-rendered virtual DOM tree.

edges.cite: Isla, Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI (GDC 2005); Behavior tree (Wikipedia)
edges.note: BTs were proposed as an improvement over HSMs for game AI: transition logic lives in tree structure, not scattered across states.
Data binding keeps view and model in sync via Observer: bound targets subscribe to source change notifications.
